title: The 8 Best Tools for AI Agents in 2026, One for Every Job
summary: The best tools for AI agents in 2026, picked by job: Monid for paid tools, AgentMail for inboxes, Browser Use, Firecrawl, HydraDB, Hyperspell, smol machines and Telnyx. Pricing and trade-offs for each.
body_markdown:
A model on its own can write and reason, and that's about it. To do a job it needs tools: a way to pay for data, an email address, a browser, something that reads the web, a memory, a safe place to run code, and sometimes a phone line. Our picks, one per job:[Monid](https://monid.ai/openrouter-for-agent-tools) for paid tools behind a single key, AgentMail for inboxes, Browser Use for browsers, Firecrawl for web data, HydraDB for memory, Hyperspell for company context, smol machines for sandboxes and Telnyx for voice. We build AgentMail and work with several of the others, so read the disclosure inHow we picked before you trust the ranking.


TL;DR


1. **Monid** : best for giving an agent thousands of paid tools behind one key and one wallet
2. **AgentMail** : best for giving each agent its own email inbox
3. **Browser Use** : best for agents that have to click through real websites
4. **Firecrawl** : best for turning web pages into text an agent can read
5. **HydraDB** : best for long-term agent memory you can self-host
6. **Hyperspell** : best for giving agents your company's context
7. **smol machines** : best sandbox when the same VM has to run on a laptop and in the cloud
8. **Telnyx** : best for agents that make and take phone calls

## How did we pick these tools?


We picked jobs first, by asking where agents get stuck once they leave the chat window, and then one tool per job. Two rules applied to every pick. An agent has to be able to use the tool directly, through an API, SDK, MCP server or skill file, without a person driving a dashboard. And there has to be a way to start free or for a few dollars. Hyperspell breaks the second rule, because it has no public pricing, and we kept it anyway for reasons explained in its entry.


This is a vendor blog, so here is who we have a relationship with. AgentMail is our product. AgentMail is one of the providers on Monid. Telnyx gives every agent that signs up without an email address an inbox that runs on AgentMail. Firecrawl and Telnyx accept AgentID, our sign-in for agents. We run our own company brain on Hyperspell. We wrote each entry the way we'd want ours written, with the weak spots included. Prices come from each vendor's pricing page in November 2026.


If you're looking specifically for MCP servers, we compared eleven in[Best MCP servers for AI agents](https://www.agentmail.to/blog/best-mcp-servers-for-ai-agents) . For the framework the agent runs in, see[The 10 best AI agent frameworks](https://www.agentmail.to/blog/best-ai-agent-frameworks-2026) .


## 1. Monid: best for giving an agent thousands of paid tools behind one key


**What does it do?**[Monid](https://monid.ai/openrouter-for-agent-tools) sits between an agent and third-party APIs. The agent loads one skill file and draws on one wallet, and through those it can find, compare and pay for more than 3,400 tools across 71 categories: people data from Apollo and People Data Labs, search from Exa, scraping from Apify, voice from ElevenLabs, video from Seedance. Monid calls itself the OpenRouter for agent tools, and the comparison fits. You integrate once and reach every provider behind it, the way OpenRouter works for models.


**Who is it for?** Teams whose agents need data or services from many vendors and who don't want to sign up, fund a balance and rotate a key for each one.


The feature we'd point to is price routing. When several providers can answer the same task, the agent sees each one's live per-call price and picks the cheapest one that can do the job. Monid's own example is TikTok search, where TikHub charges $0.0015 per call and Apify charges $0.0057 per result. At 10,000 lookups a day, one result each, that's $15 against $57. Monid also publishes what its tested agent roles cost to run, like $0.15 per lead for an SDR agent and $0.06 per company dossier for an analyst agent.


Monid covers tools that sell data or actions per call, paid from the agent's own balance. It isn't built for signing in to your user's Gmail or Salesforce and acting as them inside their account.


### Pricing


Pay per call, priced in cents, from one prepaid balance that covers every provider. There's no subscription and no per-tool sign-up.


## 2. AgentMail: best for giving each agent its own email inbox


**What does it do?** AgentMail creates real email inboxes by API. Each agent gets its own address, sends and receives from it, and gets a webhook or WebSocket event when mail arrives. Threads, labels, attachments, drafts and search work the way they do in a person's mailbox, reachable through the Python and TypeScript SDKs, an MCP server, or IMAP and SMTP.


**Who is it for?** Agents that need to hear back from someone. A sales agent waiting on a reply, a support agent working a queue, or any agent signing up for a service that emails it a verification code.


That last case is why email shows up underneath so many other tools on this list. Accounts are tied to email addresses. An agent that borrows a person's Gmail gets that person's whole inbox, their two-factor prompts, and a real chance of a ban when Google flags the automation. An agent with its own inbox can sign up for a tool, read the confirmation code, and carry on. Telnyx reached the same conclusion from the other side: every agent that signs up for Telnyx without an email address now gets an inbox[powered by AgentMail](https://www.agentmail.to/blog/every-ai-agent-on-telnyx-gets-an-inbox) .


We also run[AgentID](https://www.agentid.com/) , a standard OpenID Connect provider where the agent's inbox is its identity. An app adds it next to "Sign in with Google," and the agent signs in as itself while the app can still see which person owns it. Firecrawl, Telnyx, Turso and Supermemory accept it.


AgentMail is priced per inbox, which suits agents that hold conversations. If your agent only sends one-way notifications at high volume, a sending API like Resend or Postmark will cost less per email.


### Pricing


The free plan includes 3 inboxes, 3,000 emails a month (100 a day) and a custom domain, with no card. Developer is $20 a month for 10 inboxes, Startup is $200 a month for 150, and Enterprise is custom. AgentID is free for apps that accept it.


## 3. Browser Use: best for agents that have to click through real websites


**What does it do?** Browser Use gives agents a browser. Its open-source agent library has about 122,000 stars on GitHub. The cloud product adds hosted web agents, where you send a task and get JSON back, and stealth browsers with CAPTCHA handling and residential proxies for sites that block bots. Browser Harness, a free and open-source tool layer, hands coding agents like Claude Code and Codex direct browser actions: open a tab, click a coordinate, run JavaScript on the page.


**Who is it for?** Agents whose work sits behind a login or a form with no API. Procurement portals, booking flows, government sites, checkout pages.


Browser Use publishes its own benchmarks, so read them as a vendor's numbers. Its stealth browsers got through on 90.5% of visits in a test across 100 sites, and Browser Use Cloud completed 95.8% of a 500-task shopping benchmark.


A browser is also the slowest and most expensive way to fetch a page that has an API or loads with a plain request. Use it for actions, and send plain reads to Firecrawl. When a sign-up flow ends in a verification email, the agent needs somewhere to receive it, which we cover in[giving a Browser Use agent its own inbox](https://www.agentmail.to/blog/agentmail-browser-use-full-web-email) .


Also worth a look: Browserbase, whose free tier includes one browser hour and whose open-source Stagehand framework suits teams that want to write the automation themselves.


### Pricing


$1 of free credit to start, which doesn't expire. Stealth browsers cost $0.06 per browser-hour and hosted web agents a median $0.006 per task. Browser Harness is free.


## 4. Firecrawl: best for turning web pages into text an agent can read


**What does it do?** Firecrawl converts web pages into clean text and structured data that fit in a context window. Scrape pulls one page, Crawl walks a whole site, Map lists a site's URLs, and Search runs a web search and returns the content of the results. Newer endpoints cover browser sessions (Interact), change detection (Monitor) and an Agent endpoint that's still in preview.


**Who is it for?** Research agents, retrieval pipelines, and any agent that needs to read the web rather than act on it.


The reason to reach for Firecrawl before a browser is cost. A scrape costs one credit and comes back as markdown. Getting the same page through a browser agent means loading and rendering it, and usually paying for model calls to decide where to click. On the free plan, 1,000 credits a month covers roughly 1,000 scraped pages or 500 searches.


Firecrawl is open source, and it accepts AgentID, so an agent with its own inbox can sign in to Firecrawl without a person completing the sign-up for it.


Firecrawl reads pages. It doesn't log in, fill forms or press buttons, which is Browser Use's job. And if the hard part is finding the right pages rather than extracting them, look at Exa, a search engine built for agents, which starts at $4 per 1,000 searches and gives you $10 of free credit each month.


### Pricing


Free: 1,000 credits a month, no card. Hobby is $16 a month billed annually ($19 billed monthly) for 5,000 credits, and Standard is $83 ($99) for 100,000.


## 5. HydraDB: best for long-term agent memory you can self-host


**What does it do?** HydraDB stores what an agent accumulates, such as documents, past conversations and decisions, as a graph on object storage. It maps how those pieces relate and serves the relevant ones back to the agent over an API or MCP. It's open source and runs against any S3-compatible store, with a managed cloud for teams that don't want to operate it.


**Who is it for?** Agents that work across days or weeks and need to recall what came before. An account manager agent that remembers the last three calls with a customer. A support agent that knows this customer already reported the bug in March.


HydraDB reports 90.79% on LongMemEval-S and 91.4% Recall@10 on FinanceBench. Both are its own numbers. Building on object storage is how it claims costs 10 to 100 times lower than the alternatives, which is plausible for large, cold memory and worth testing against your own access pattern.


Email is one of the obvious things for an agent to remember. The` hydradb-agentmail-plugin` connector copies an agent's mail into HydraDB, keyed on each message's Message-ID so a re-sync updates records instead of duplicating them, and the agent then searches past threads in HydraDB instead of paging through its inbox. The[setup takes three commands](https://www.agentmail.to/blog/agentmail-hydradb-integration) .


The free version is self-hosted with community support. If you don't want to run it, the managed plan has a $25 monthly minimum. Supermemory is the other memory API we'd look at, and it also accepts AgentID.


### Pricing


Self-hosted is free. The managed Ship plan has a $25 monthly minimum, with storage at $0.50 per GB-month. Scale has a $300 minimum and adds a separate database per customer.


## 6. Hyperspell: best for giving agents your company's context


**What does it do?** Hyperspell connects to the tools a company already runs on, with more than 50 connectors including Slack, Gmail, Google Drive, Notion, Linear, Jira, Salesforce, HubSpot and GitHub. It builds a graph of the people, projects and decisions in those tools and exposes it to agents as a filesystem they can read. Permissions are inherited from each source.


**Who is it for?** Internal agents and coding agents that keep needing answers a teammate would know, like who owns an account or what was agreed on last week's call.


HydraDB holds what an agent writes down as it works. Hyperspell holds what your company has already written down in other tools, and keeps it in sync as those tools change.


We kept Hyperspell on the list without public pricing because we use it. AgentMail's company brain pulls from Notion, Slack, GitHub, Stripe, PostHog, our meeting notes, our support tool and our lifecycle email inboxes, and anyone on the team can point Claude or Codex at it and ask.


### Pricing


Not published. Hyperspell sells through a demo and states SOC 2 certification and GDPR compliance.


## 7. smol machines: best sandbox when the same VM runs locally and in the cloud


**What does it do?** smol machines runs agent code inside hardware-isolated Linux microVMs. Each workload gets its own guest kernel through macOS Hypervisor, Linux KVM or Windows Hypervisor Platform, and a machine boots in under 200ms. The same machine, packaged as a single` .smolmachine` file, runs on a laptop, in smol cloud, or on your own servers.


**Who is it for?** Teams running code their agent wrote and nobody reviewed, who want VM-level isolation and are tired of the dev sandbox behaving differently from production.


Fast boot is common among sandbox providers now. Portability is less common, and it's what smol machines is built around: a machine that works in` smolvm` on a MacBook should run unchanged in the cloud. Memory is elastic through a virtio balloon, so the host commits only what the guest uses, and the default machine gets 4 vCPUs and 8 GiB of RAM.


Whatever sandbox you pick, the agent's email and its accounts should live outside it. A microVM is disposable by design, and a verification code sent to an address inside one disappears with it.


The other sandbox we'd evaluate is E2B. Its free Hobby tier caps sessions at one hour and Pro ($150 a month plus usage) raises that to 24 hours, which matters for any agent that waits on a person.


### Pricing


New accounts get $100 of prepaid credit that doesn't expire. After that it's usage-based, billed to the second with a one-minute minimum: $0.04 per running machine-hour, $0.05 per vCPU-hour and $0.0162 per GB-hour of memory. A stopped machine only pays for disk. The Standard plan has no monthly fee and allows 20 machines, and Pro is $20 a month plus usage for 100.


## 8. Telnyx: best for agents that make and take phone calls


**What does it do?** Telnyx is a carrier with its own network, and it sells what a voice agent needs through one API: phone numbers, SMS, calling, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and a voice AI engine that handles turn-taking, interruptions, tool calls and knowledge base lookups. It also runs LLM inference on its own GPUs.


**Who is it for?** Agents that answer support lines, book appointments or call suppliers, built by teams who'd rather buy the number, the speech models and the orchestration from one company than wire three together.


Telnyx is betting that agents will provision this stack themselves: buy a number, send a text, place a call. An agent doing that needs an identity of its own, which is why every agent that signs up for Telnyx without an email address now gets a Telnyx Agent Inbox powered by AgentMail, and why Telnyx accepts AgentID sign-in.


The voice engine bills in 60-second increments, so a 10-second call costs a full minute. If your agent makes lots of short calls, model the bill before you commit. Teams that would rather run the media layer themselves should look at LiveKit, the open-source framework for real-time voice agents.


### Pricing


The voice engine costs $0.05 a minute, which includes orchestration, speech-to-text and text-to-speech. Telnyx estimates a production agent at about $0.06 a minute once LLM tokens and telephony are added. US local inbound calls start at $0.0032 a minute.

## How do you choose tools for an AI agent?


Start from the step where your agent currently fails, and buy the tool for that step.


If it stalls on a verification email or never sees the customer's reply, it needs an inbox of its own. If it already has a key for one data vendor and now needs four more, route those calls through Monid instead of signing up four times. If it needs to read a page, use Firecrawl, and switch to Browser Use only when it has to log in and click. If it forgets what happened on Tuesday, add HydraDB. If it doesn't know what your company knows, add Hyperspell. If it writes code you haven't read, run that code in a sandbox. If customers call it, give it a Telnyx number.


There's one more test worth running on any tool before you commit: can the agent get started without you? Tools that accept AgentID, or that sell per call through Monid, let an agent create its own access in the middle of a task. Tools that require a person to click through a dashboard or book a demo add a manual step to every new agent you deploy, and that step grows with the size of your fleet.
